title: Stir up the gift (2 Timothy 1:6)
hook: Paul tells Timothy to stir up the grace given by the laying on of hands

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christians grieve, but not as others without hope. Your line was grieve with hope. Who did you remember? Day five hundred ninety-five.

Before matches, nobody wanted to start a fire from nothing every morning. So at night people banked the hearth: they raked ash over the last coals and left them. In the morning, the fire looked dead. But you'd brush back the ash, blow gently, add a little kindling, and the flame came back. Paul uses that picture in a letter to Timothy, his young friend and co-worker, written, the letter says, from prison, near the end of Paul's life.
screen: `A HEARTH BANKED FOR THE NIGHT.` → `BLOW ON THE COALS.` → `A LETTER TO A YOUNG FRIEND.`

segments.voice: He starts with family. He remembers Timothy's faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Faith passed down a kitchen table, two generations deep. Then: "For which cause I admonish thee, that thou stir up the grace of God which is in thee, by the imposition of my hands." Stir up is one Greek word, anazōpyrein, built on the word for a live coal. Rekindle. Fan back into flame. Paul isn't telling Timothy to get a new gift. He already has it. He's telling him not to let it sit under the ash. Then the next line: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear: but of power, and of love, and of sobriety." Sobriety here means a sound mind, self-control. Timothy seems to have been timid, and Paul knows fear is what banks a fire. Catholics read the imposition of hands as the sign of ordination. In the sacrament of holy orders, the bishop lays his hands on the head of the one being ordained, in silence, and prays the prayer of consecration. The Church teaches that ordination marks a person permanently: the gift isn't lost. But it can be neglected, and so can every gift. Catholics speak the same way about the graces of baptism and confirmation. They were given once, but they need breath. Notice the order: given by God, then stirred up by the person. Paul expects Timothy to do the blowing. Grace isn't a fire you light alone. But it's also not a fire that tends itself.
screen: `LOIS, EUNICE, TIMOTHY.` · `REKINDLE: A LIVE COAL.` · `NOT THE SPIRIT OF FEAR.` · `THE LAYING ON OF HANDS.` · then, large: `STIR UP THE GRACE OF GOD WHICH IS IN THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the coal. Settle, and breathe. Think of one gift you have that's gone quiet under the ash. A way you used to pray. A skill you stopped using. A kind of patience or courage you once had. Picture it as a coal: still warm, not dead. Now picture blowing on it, gently. What's one small piece of kindling you could add today? Ten minutes. One phone call. One page. If you pray, you can ask for help to stir it up. If you don't, simply decide on the kindling. The bell holds the time.
Stir up the gift. Paul to Timothy: rekindle the grace given by the laying on of hands, like coals under ash brought back to flame. Today's word.

Your line: stir up the gift. Today, use one gift you've let go quiet, even for ten minutes. And that's week eighty-five: rejoice always, whatsoever things are true, content, put on mercy, pray without ceasing, not as others without hope, and stir up the gift. Day five hundred ninety-five.
screen: `WEEK EIGHTY-FIVE: REJOICE · TRUE · CONTENT · MERCY · PRAYER · HOPE · GIFT`

howItsDone: In the Catholic rite of ordination, the bishop silently lays his hands on the head of each candidate and then prays the prayer of consecration; Catholics also speak of stirring up the graces of baptism and confirmation.

fork.setup: you're Timothy. you have a gift from God, but you've grown timid and it's gone dim. what does Paul tell you?
options: stir up the grace that's already in you.
give the work to someone bolder.
fork.reveal: "stir up the grace of God which is in thee": "God hath not given us the spirit of fear."

original.note: Greek: to rekindle, to fan into flame; built on zōpyron, a live coal (2 Timothy 1:6).

trapdoor: what it means: a gift already given by God needs to be fanned back into flame.
what a scholar hears: anazōpyrein, a live coal; the laying on of hands as the sign of ordination; an indelible character that can still be neglected.

notes: Authorship of the pastoral letters: the Church's tradition ascribes them to Paul; many modern scholars think a later follower wrote them. The voice says 'the letter says' about the prison setting. Keeper may wish to add a line.
Rite of ordination: silent laying on of hands, then the prayer of consecration (CCC 1573); indelible character (CCC 1582–1583). Confirm.
